back: Major SSI: Significant pus, systemic signs (pyrexia, tachycardia), requires drainage. Minor SSI: Discharge of pus or serous fluid without systemic illness or excessive discomfort.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus... The patient may have systemic signs such as tachycardia, pyrexia... Minor wound infections... are not associated with excessive discomfort, systemic signs.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: A post-trauma patient presents with severe local wound pain, crepitus, and a brown sweet-smelling exudate. Diagnosis?
back: Gas Gangrene (caused by Clostridium perfringens).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues... The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Why must surgeons assess the patient's systemic white cell count and heart rate when suspecting SSI?
back: To identify systemic signs (tachycardia, raised WBC) that distinguish a major SSI from a localized minor infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): The patient may have systemic signs such as tachycardia, pyrexia and a raised white cell count.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Identify the criteria for Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) in surgical sepsis.
back: Two or more of: 1. Temp >38°C or <36°C; 2. Heart rate >90/min; 3. Resp rate >20/min; 4. WBC >12 or <4 x 10^9/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): Table 5.3 SIRS is Two of: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C); tachycardia (>90/min); tachypnoea (>20/min); white cell count >12 or <4 x 10^9/litre.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: What is the typical time delay for a surgical wound abscess to present clinically?
back: 7 to 10 days post-surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): Most abscesses relating to surgical wounds take 7–10 days to form after surgery.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Differentiate between the clinical appearance of Cellulitis and Lymphangitis.
back: Cellulitis: Spreading, non-suppurative, poorly localized erythema. Lymphangitis: Painful red streaks tracking along lymphatics toward regional nodes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page)-70: Cellulitis is a non-suppurative, invasive infection... spreading inflammation... Lymphangitis presents as painful red streaks in affected lymphatics draining the source.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Define the clinical hallmarks of Synergistic Spreading Gangrene (Necrotizing Fasciitis).
back: Severe wound pain, signs of spreading inflammation, crepitus, and a characteristic foul smell; subdermal spread is more extensive than visible skin changes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): Severe wound pain, signs of spreading inflammation with crepitus and smell... The subdermal spread of gangrene is always much more extensive than appears from initial examination.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Which early clinical feature distinguishes invasive cellulitis from a simple wound abscess?
back: Invasive cellulitis typically presents earlier (3–4 days post-op) and is non-suppurative/spreading, whereas abscesses take longer (7–10 days) and are localized/suppurative.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Suppurative wound infections take 7–10 days to develop, and even cellulitis around wounds... takes 3–4 days to develop.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What are the four cardinal local clinical features of an SSI (Celsus signs)?
back:
- Calor (heat)
- Rubor (redness)
- Dolor (pain)
- Tumor (swelling)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): An abscess presents all the clinical features of acute inflammation originally described by Celsus: calor (heat), rubor (redness), dolor (pain) and tumor (swelling).

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: How do systemic signs differentiate a Major SSI from a Minor SSI?
back:
- Major SSI: Significant pus, tachycardia, pyrexia, and raised white cell count.
- Minor SSI: Serous discharge/pus without systemic signs or excessive discomfort.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus... The patient may have systemic signs such as tachycardia, pyrexia and a raised white cell count.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the typical postoperative timeframe for the appearance of wound cellulitis?
back: Typically takes 3–4 days to develop post-surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): ...even cellulitis around wounds caused by invasive organisms (such as b-haemolytic Streptococcus) takes 3–4 days to develop.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Which two clinical findings are hallmark early indicators of Gas Gangrene?
back:
- Severe local wound pain
- Crepitus (gas in tissues)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues).

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What specific appearance of wound exudate suggests a Clostridium perfringens infection?
back: Thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate, in which Gram staining will reveal bacteria.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Define the clinical criteria for Sepsis in a surgical patient.
back: SIRS (Temp >38°C/<36°C, HR >90, RR >20, or abnormal WBC) plus a documented infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): Sepsis is SIRS with a documented infection. SIRS is Two of: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C), tachycardia (>90/min), tachypnoea (>20/min), white cell count >12 or <4.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the characteristic clinical progression of Lymphangitis?
back: Painful red streaks in the skin extending toward regional lymph nodes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): Lymphangitis is part of a similar process and presents as painful red streaks in affected lymphatics draining the source of infection.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Why might Necrotising Fasciitis be deceptively extensive on clinical examination?
back: Subdermal spread of gangrene is significantly wider than visible skin changes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): The subdermal spread of gangrene is always much more extensive than appears from initial examination.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the usual time interval for a postoperative wound abscess to form?
back: Most form 7–10 days after the surgical procedure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): Most abscesses relating to surgical wounds take 7–10 days to form after surgery.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What microscopic component of pus indicates a pyogenic bacterial infection?
back: Dead and dying neutrophils (white blood cells).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): Pus is composed of dead and dying white blood cells, predominantly neutrophils, that have succumbed to bacterial toxins.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What are the four cardinal clinical features of acute inflammation in a localized SSI (Celsus)?
back:
1. Calor (heat)
2. Rubor (redness)
3. Dolor (pain)
4. Tumor (swelling)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [An abscess presents all the clinical features of acute inflammation originally described by Celsus: calor (heat), rubor (redness), dolor (pain) and tumor (swelling).]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What physiological mechanism causes severe pain in a localized surgical abscess?
back: The abscess contains hyperosmolar material that draws in fluid, increasing internal pressure and stimulating pain receptors.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Abscesses contain hyperosmolar material that draws in fluid. This increases the pressure and causes pain.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: How is a 'major' SSI clinically distinguished from a 'minor' SSI?
back: Major SSIs involve significant pus discharge and systemic signs (tachycardia, pyrexia), whereas minor SSIs lack systemic illness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus spontaneously or needs a secondary procedure to drain it. The patient may have systemic signs such as tachycardia, pyrexia...]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Which early clinical features specifically suggest Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) in a wound?
back:
1. Severe local wound pain
2. Crepitus (gas in tissues)
3. Thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): [Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus... The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate...]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Compare the typical early onset timing of streptococcal cellulitis vs. suppurative wound infections.
back:
1. Cellulitis (invasive organisms): 3–4 days post-op.
2. Suppurative infections (abscess): 7–10 days post-op.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Suppurative wound infections take 7–10 days to develop, and even cellulitis around wounds caused by invasive organisms (such as b-haemolytic Streptococcus) takes 3–4 days to develop.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What are the clinical systemic parameters required to diagnose SIRS in a surgical patient?
back:
1. Temp >38°C or <36°C
2. Heart rate >90/min
3. Respiratory rate >20/min
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [Table 5.3: SIRS is... hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C), tachycardia (>90/min) or tachypnoea (>20/min)]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What early clinical finding indicates lymphangitis following a surgical site infection?
back: Painful red streaks in the affected lymphatics draining the infection source.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): [Lymphangitis... presents as painful red streaks in affected lymphatics draining the source of infection.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Which features suggest necrotizing fasciitis rather than simple cellulitis?
back: Severe pain out of proportion to signs, crepitus, foul smell, and subdermal spread beyond visible skin margins.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): [Severe wound pain, signs of spreading inflammation with crepitus and smell are all signs of the infection spreading... The subdermal spread of gangrene is always much more extensive than appears...]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the clinical significance of 'functio laesa' in the context of SSI?
back: Loss of function; the patient avoids using the infected part because of pain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [To these can be added functio laesa (loss of function: if it hurts, the infected part is not used).]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What defines a 'Deep SSI' according to classification systems?
back: Infection involving the deeper musculofascial layers of the surgical site.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): [The other categories include deep SSI (infection in the deeper musculofascial layers) and organ space infection...]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What are the four cardinal clinical signs of localized infection described by Celsus?
back:
1. Calor (heat)
2. Rubor (redness)
3. Dolor (pain)
4. Tumor (swelling)
*Note: Functio laesa (loss of function) is often added.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [An abscess presents all the clinical features of acute inflammation originally described by Celsus: calor (heat), rubor (redness), dolor (pain) and tumor (swelling). To these can be added functio laesa (loss of function)]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Why do abscesses cause increasing localized pressure and pain?
back: Abscesses contain hyperosmolar material that draws in fluid, which increases internal pressure and stimulates pain receptors.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Abscesses contain hyperosmolar material that draws in fluid. This increases the pressure and causes pain.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What defines a 'major' Surgical Site Infection (SSI) compared to a minor one?
back:
1. Significant discharge of pus
2. Requires secondary drainage procedure
3. Presence of systemic signs (tachycardia, pyrexia)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus spontaneously or needs a secondary procedure to drain it. The patient may have systemic signs such as tachycardia, pyrexia and a raised white cell count.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: A post-op wound shows severe pain, crepitus, and a sweet-smelling brown exudate. What is the diagnosis?
back: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): [Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues)... The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Define the 'decisive period' in the context of preventing surgical site infection.
back: The 4-hour interval after tissue breach before bacterial growth is established; prophylactic antibiotics must be present in tissues during this window.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established enough to cause an infection after a breach in the tissues... This interval is called the ‘decisive period’.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the typical timeframe for a surgical wound abscess to manifest after surgery?
back: 7–10 days postoperatively.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Most abscesses relating to surgical wounds take 7–10 days to form after surgery.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: How does cellulitis differ from an abscess in its early clinical presentation?
back: Cellulitis is a non-suppurative, poorly localized, and invasive spreading infection, whereas an abscess is localized and contains pus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Cellulitis is a non-suppurative, invasive infection of tissues... There is poor localisation in addition to the cardinal signs of spreading inflammation.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What feature distinguishes Necrotizing Fasciitis from cellulitis on clinical examination?
back:
1. Pain out of proportion to clinical signs
2. Crepitus and foul smell
3. Rapidly spreading subdermal gangrene
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): [Severe wound pain, signs of spreading inflammation with crepitus and smell are all signs of the infection spreading. Untreated, it will lead to widespread local gangrene...]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What systemic response occurs when bacterial endotoxins trigger excessive cytokine release?
back: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [SIRS is a systemic manifestation of sepsis... secondary peritonitis, may lead to SIRS through the release of lipopolysaccharide endotoxin... toxins stimulate the release of cytokines from macrophages.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the primary cellular composition of surgical pus?
back: Dead and dying white blood cells, predominantly neutrophils.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Pus is composed of dead and dying white blood cells, predominantly neutrophils, that have succumbed to bacterial toxins.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What are the five cardinal clinical signs of a localized surgical site infection (abscess)?
back:
- Calor (heat)
- Rubor (redness)
- Dolor (pain)
- Tumor (swelling)
- Functio laesa (loss of function)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [An abscess presents all the clinical features of acute inflammation originally described by Celsus: calor (heat), rubor (redness), dolor (pain) and tumor (swelling). To these can be added functio laesa (loss of function).]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the primary physiological mechanism causing pain in a developing surgical abscess?
back:
- Presence of hyperosmolar material
- Influx of fluid via osmosis
- Increased internal pressure stretching tissues
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Abscesses contain hyperosmolar material that draws in fluid. This increases the pressure and causes pain.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Contrast the clinical defining features of a 'Major' vs. 'Minor' Surgical Site Infection (SSI).
back:
- Major SSI: Significant pus, systemic illness (fever/tachycardia), or requires re-intervention.
- Minor SSI: Serous/infected discharge, minimal discomfort, no systemic signs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus spontaneously or needs a secondary procedure to drain it. The patient may have systemic signs... Minor wound infections may discharge pus or infected serous fluid but are not associated with excessive discomfort [or] systemic signs.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: A post-op patient has severe wound pain, crepitus, and a brown, sweet-smelling exudate. What is the diagnosis?
back:
- Gas Gangrene
- Pathogen: Clostridium perfringens
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): [Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues... The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the 'decisive period' in surgical infection prevention?
back:
- The 4-hour window post-tissue breach
- Period before bacterial growth is established
- Timeframe when prophylactic antibiotics are effective
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established enough to cause an infection... This interval is called the ‘decisive period’.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: According to the Southampton system, what specifically defines a Grade IV SSI?
back:
- Presence of pus
- Subdivided by length: IVa (≤2 cm) or IVb (>2 cm)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Table 5.1 Southampton wound grading system: IV Pus; IVa At one point only (≤2 cm); IVb Along wound (>2 cm)]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Compare the typical time to presentation for post-operative cellulitis versus a wound abscess.
back:
- Cellulitis: 3–4 days post-surgery
- Abscess: 7–10 days post-surgery
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Suppurative wound infections take 7–10 days to develop, and even cellulitis around wounds caused by invasive organisms... takes 3–4 days to develop.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What feature distinguishes Synergistic Spreading Gangrene (Necrotizing Fasciitis) from simple cellulitis?
back:
- Extensive subdermal spread (greater than visible skin signs)
- Dishwater/foul smell
- Systemic multi-organ failure
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): [The subdermal spread of gangrene is always much more extensive than appears from initial examination... signs of spreading inflammation with crepitus and smell... systemic multisystem organ failure.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What systemic vital sign criteria define Sepsis in the context of a documented surgical infection?
back:
- Temperature: >38°C or <36°C
- Heart Rate: >90 bpm
- Respiratory Rate: >20/min
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [Table 5.3: SIRS is Two of: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C); tachycardia (>90/min); tachypnoea (>20/min). Sepsis is SIRS with a documented infection.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Define the anatomic depth of a Deep Surgical Site Infection.
back:
- Involves deeper musculofascial layers
- Does not include organ space
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): [The other categories include deep SSI (infection in the deeper musculofascial layers) and organ space infection (such as an abdominal abscess).]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What are the four classic local clinical features of an abscess (Celsus)?
back:
1. Calor (heat)
2. Rubor (redness)
3. Dolor (pain)
4. Tumor (swelling)
*Bonus: Functio laesa (loss of function)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [An abscess presents all the clinical features of acute inflammation originally described by Celsus: calor (heat), rubor (redness), dolor (pain) and tumor (swelling). To these can be added functio laesa (loss of function)]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiology causing systemic signs (toxaemia) in early non-suppurative surgical infections.
back:
1. Bacterial toxins are released into the circulation.
2. Toxins stimulate a cytokine-mediated systemic inflammatory response.
3. Clinical result: Chills, fever, and rigors, even if blood cultures are negative.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): [These events follow the release of toxins into the circulation, which stimulate a cytokine-mediated systemic inflammatory response even though blood cultures may be negative. ... common, with chills, fever and rigors.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Contrast the clinical presentation of Major vs. Minor Surgical Site Infections (SSIs).
back:
1. Major SSI: Significant pus discharge, requires drainage, and systemic illness (fever, tachycardia).
2. Minor SSI: Infected serous fluid/minor pus, no systemic signs, no delay in discharge.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus spontaneously or needs a secondary procedure to drain it. The patient may have systemic signs ... Minor wound infections ... are not associated with excessive discomfort, systemic signs or delay in return home]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Patient presents 4 days post-op with spreading erythema and tachycardia but no pus. Diagnosis?
back:
Cellulitis.
- Characteristics: Non-suppurative, invasive, poorly localised spreading inflammation.
- Common timing: 3–4 days post-operation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page)-74: [Cellulitis is a non-suppurative, invasive infection of tissues ... typically caused by organisms such as b-haemolytic streptococci ... even cellulitis around wounds ... takes 3–4 days to develop.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the pharmacological 'decisive period' for preventing surgical site infections?
back:
1. The 4-hour window after tissue breach (trauma/surgery).
2. Antibiotic tissue levels must exceed the MIC90 during this interval to prevent established bacterial growth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established enough to cause an infection ... This interval is called the ‘decisive period’ ... prophylactic antibiotics should be given to cover this period]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What are the clinical criteria for diagnosing SIRS in a surgical patient?
back:
Two or more of:
1. Hyperthermia (>38°C) or Hypothermia (<36°C)
2. Tachycardia (>90/min)
3. Tachypnoea (>20/min)
4. WBC count >12 or <4 x 10^9/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [SIRS is Two of: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C); tachycardia (>90/min...); tachypnoea (>20/min); white cell count >12 x 10 9 /litre or <4 x 10 9 /litre]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Compare the typical post-operative onset timing for cellulitis versus wound abscesses.
back:
1. Cellulitis: Typically 3–4 days post-operation.
2. Wound Abscesses: Typically 7–10 days post-operation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Suppurative wound infections take 7–10 days to develop, and even cellulitis around wounds caused by invasive organisms ... takes 3–4 days to develop.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Which specific clinical findings differentiate gas gangrene from other SSIs?
back:
1. Severe local wound pain.
2. Crepitus (gas in tissues).
3. Thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate.
4. Spreading gangrene and circulatory collapse.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): [Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus ... The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate ... spreading gangrene follow ... Early systemic complications with circulatory collapse]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: How does the physiological 'translocation' loop lead to MODS in surgical patients?
back:
1. Gut failure/starvation causes bacterial translocation to mesenteric nodes.
2. Endotoxins (LPS) are released.
3. Excessive proinflammatory cytokine release (IL-1, TNF) damages remote organs, causing dysfunction (MODS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page)-72: [translocate to the mesenteric nodes and cause the release of endotoxins ... through the excessive release of proinflammatory cytokines ... damage it, leading to increased vascular permeability ... picture of multiple organ dysfunction syndrome or MODS.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What clinical finding defines the presence of 'suppuration' in a wound?
back:
The production of pus (pus bonum et laudabile).
Pus consists of dead/dying white blood cells (neutrophils) and necrotic tissue debris.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 63 (Book Page)-69: [Galen recognised that this localisation of infection (suppuration) in wounds ... often heralded recovery ... Pus is composed of dead and dying white blood cells, predominantly neutrophils, that have succumbed to bacterial toxins.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: What are the four classic cardinal local signs of inflammation in a surgical site infection?
back:
1. Calor (heat)
2. Rubor (redness)
3. Dolor (pain)
4. Tumor (swelling)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): An abscess presents all the clinical features of acute inflammation originally described by Celsus: calor (heat), rubor (redness), dolor (pain) and tumor (swelling).

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: What is the typical timeframe for the clinical presentation of cellulitis versus suppurative wound infections?
back:
1. Cellulitis: 3–4 days post-surgery.
2. Suppurative infections: 7–10 days post-surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Suppurative wound infections take 7–10 days to develop, and even cellulitis around wounds caused by invasive organisms (such as b-haemolytic Streptococcus) takes 3–4 days to develop.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: How is a Major Surgical Site Infection (SSI) clinically distinguished from a Minor SSI?
back: Major SSI involves significant pus discharge, systemic illness (pyrexia, tachycardia), or requires a secondary drainage procedure. Minor SSIs lack systemic signs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus spontaneously or needs a secondary procedure to drain it. The patient may have systemic signs such as tachycardia, pyrexia and a raised white cell count.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Identify the early clinical hallmarks of gas gangrene in a surgical or traumatic wound.
back:
1. Severe local pain
2. Crepitus (gas in tissues)
3. Thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate
4. Rapid systemic circulatory collapse
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus... The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: What are the early systemic indicators of 'toxaemia' following the release of bacterial toxins?
back:
1. Chills
2. Fever
3. Rigors
These follow cytokine-mediated responses to circulating toxins.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): Systemic signs (the old-fashioned term is toxaemia) are common, with chills, fever and rigors. These events follow the release of toxins into the circulation, which stimulate a cytokine-mediated systemic inflammatory response.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: What clinical criteria define Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) in a surgical patient?
back:
1. Temp >38°C or <36°C
2. Heart rate >90/min
3. Respiratory rate >20/min
4. WBC >12 or <4 x 10^9/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): Table 5.3: SIRS is Two of: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C); tachycardia (>90/min...); tachypnoea (>20/min); white cell count >12... or <4.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: What does the clinical sign 'functio laesa' indicate in an infected surgical site?
back: Loss of function; the patient avoids moving or using the infected part due to pain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): To these can be added functio laesa (loss of function: if it hurts, the infected part is not used).

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Contrast the early local presentation of Necrotizing Fasciitis with simple wound cellulitis.
back: Necrotizing Fasciitis presents with pain out of proportion to appearance, rapid subdermal spread, crepitus, foul smell, and early systemic organ failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): Severe wound pain, signs of spreading inflammation with crepitus and smell are all signs... The subdermal spread of gangrene is always much more extensive than appears.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Why do surgical abscesses cause progressive, localized pain before drainage?
back: Abscesses contain hyperosmolar material that draws in fluid, increasing internal pressure on tissues.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): Abscesses contain hyperosmolar material that draws in fluid. This increases the pressure and causes pain.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: What are the characteristic clinical features of lymphangitis draining a surgical infection?
back: Painful red streaks extending toward regional lymph nodes, often accompanied by tender lymphadenopathy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): Lymphangitis... presents as painful red streaks in affected lymphatics draining the source of infection... accompanied by painful lymph node groups.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What is the gold-standard initial management for a localized surgical abscess?
back:
● Incision and drainage (I&D).
● If left open to drain freely, antibiotics are generally unnecessary.
● Antibiotics are indicated if the cavity is closed primarily.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): Abscesses need drainage... When the cavity is left open to drain freely, there is no need for antibiotic therapy as well.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
coreConcept: The Decisive Period for Antibiotic Prophylaxis
front: Q: Define the 'decisive period' in the context of surgical infection prevention.
back:
● The 4-hour interval after tissue breach before bacterial growth is established.
● Prophylactic antibiotics must reach tissue levels above MIC90 during this window to be effective.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): This interval is called the ‘decisive period’ and strategies aimed at preventing infection from taking a hold become ineffective after this time period.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Contrast the definitions of 'antiseptic' versus 'aseptic' surgical techniques.
back:
● Antiseptic: Killing bacteria on the skin surface before surgical incision.
● Aseptic: Maintaining bacteria-free environment/conditions throughout the operative procedure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): As well as killing the bacteria on the skin before surgical incision (antiseptic technique), the conditions under which the operation was performed were kept free of bacteria (aseptic technique).

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Management for a military wound with crepitus and sweet-smelling exudate?
back:
● Immediate aggressive debridement of all necrotic tissue.
● High-dose intravenous penicillin.
● Circulatory support and monitoring for organ failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): Once gas gangrene infection is established, large doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues are required.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What is the optimal pharmacological step for administering prophylactic antibiotics?
back:
● Single-shot intravenous administration at induction of anesthesia.
● Ensures maximal tissue levels before the first incision is made.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia is therefore optimal... tissue levels of the antibiotic should remain high throughout the operation.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: List the clinical criteria required to diagnose SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome).
back:
Two or more of:
● Temperature >38°C or <36°C
● Heart rate >90 bpm
● Respiratory rate >20/min
● WBC >12x10^9/L or <4x10^9/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): SIRS is Two of: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C); tachycardia (>90/min...); tachypnoea (>20/min); white cell count >12 × 10 9 /litre or <4 × 10 9 /litre

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: How should a heavily contaminated or 'dirty' wound be managed?
back:
● Delay primary closure.
● Allow the wound to granulate.
● Perform delayed primary or secondary closure later.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): Waiting for the wound to granulate and then performing a delayed primary or secondary closure may be considered a better option in such cases.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Compare the management of a breast abscess versus a pilonidal abscess.
back:
● Breast: Manage with simple needle aspiration and antibiotics.
● Pilonidal: Requires I&D and curettage; high recurrence risk if a hair nidus remains.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): Some small breast abscesses can be managed by simple needle aspiration... a pilonidal abscess has a higher recurrence risk... because a nidus of hair may remain.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Describe the metabolic loop leading from gut failure to SIRS.
back: ● Gut failure/starvation → bacterial translocation to mesenteric nodes → endotoxin release → macrophage activation → systemic cytokine release (IL-1, TNFα) → SIRS.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page)-68: bacteria... translocate to the mesenteric nodes and cause the release of endotoxins... harmful systemic inflammatory response through the excessive release of proinflammatory cytokines.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What is the most effective preoperative method for hair removal?
back:
● Hair clipping in the theatre immediately before surgery.
● Shaving the night before is contraindicated as it doubles SSI rates.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): Preoperative skin shaving should be undertaken... immediately before surgery as the SSI rate... may be doubled if shaving is performed the night before... hair clipping is best.

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What are the four cardinal clinical signs of acute inflammation in an abscess?
back: The signs include calor (heat), rubor (redness), dolor (pain), and tumor (swelling). Loss of function (functio laesa) is often added to this list.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [An abscess presents all the clinical features of acute inflammation originally described by Celsus: calor (heat), rubor (redness), dolor (pain) and tumor (swelling). To these can be added functio laesa (loss of function).]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Why does an abscess cause increasing local pressure and pain early in its formation?
back: Abscesses contain hyperosmolar material that draws in fluid through osmosis. This increases internal pressure, which directly causes pain and tension.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Abscesses contain hyperosmolar material that draws in fluid. This increases the pressure and causes pain.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: How is a 'major' SSI clinically distinguished from a 'minor' SSI?
back: Major SSI involves significant pus discharge or required drainage, often with systemic signs (pyrexia, tachycardia). Minor SSI has minimal discharge and lacks systemic illness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus spontaneously or needs a secondary procedure to drain it. The patient may have systemic signs... Minor wound infections... are not associated with excessive discomfort, systemic signs.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Which early clinical features in a trauma wound suggest gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens)?
back: 1. Severe local wound pain. 2. Crepitus (gas in tissues). 3. Thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate. 4. Spreading gangrene and oedema.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page): [Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues)... The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate... Oedema and spreading gangrene follow.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the 'decisive period' for antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent wound infection?
back: It is the 4-hour interval after tissue breach before bacterial growth establishes infection. Antibiotics must be present in tissues before this window closes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established enough to cause an infection after a breach in the tissues... This interval is called the 'decisive period'.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What are the four clinical criteria used to define SIRS in a surgical patient?
back: Two or more of: 1. Temp >38C or <36C. 2. Heart rate >90/min. 3. Respiratory rate >20/min. 4. WBC >12 or <4 (x10^9/L).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [SIRS is Two of: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C); tachycardia (>90/min...); tachypnoea (>20/min); white cell count >12 x 10^9/litre or <4 x 10^9/litre.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: How does the presence of a foreign body, like a silk suture, affect infection risk?
back: It reduces the critical number of organisms (inoculum size) required to initiate an infection by a logarithmic margin.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [If there is a silk suture in tissue, the critical number of organisms needed to start an infection is reduced logarithmically.]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Distinguish early cellulitis from an early abscess in a postoperative patient.
back: Cellulitis is non-suppurative, spreading, and poorly localized with systemic toxins. An abscess is a localized, suppurative collection taking 7-10 days to form.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Cellulitis is a non-suppurative, invasive infection of tissues... poor localisation... Abscesses usually follow a puncture wound... localisation of infection (suppuration).]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: Which specific proinflammatory cytokines mediate multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) in sepsis?
back: The primary mediators are Interleukin-1 (IL-1) and Tumour Necrosis Factor alpha (TNF-alpha), which stimulate neutrophil adhesion and damage to distant vascular endothelium.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) in SIRS are mediated by the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNFa).]

category: Identify early clinical features suggestive of a surgical site infection
front: Q: What is the typical timeframe for a post-surgical suppurative wound infection to develop?
back: Suppurative wound abscesses typically take 7 to 10 days to form, meaning many present after the patient has been discharged.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Most abscesses relating to surgical wounds take 7–10 days to form after surgery. As many as 75% of SSIs present after the patient has left hospital.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What is the gold standard surgical management for a localized abscess?
back:
1. Incision and drainage (I&D)
2. Curettage of the cavity walls
3. Healing by secondary intention (leave open)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Abscesses need drainage... Abscess cavities need cleaning out after incision and drainage and are traditionally encouraged to heal by secondary intention.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Define the 'decisive period' for antibiotic prophylaxis and its clinical significance.
back: The 4-hour window post-tissue breach before bacterial growth establishes. Antibiotics must reach tissue levels exceeding MIC90 during this period.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [This interval is called the ‘decisive period’ and strategies aimed at preventing infection... become ineffective after this time period.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Contrast antibiotic requirements for open vs. closed abscess drainage.
back:
1. Open drainage: Antibiotics usually unnecessary.
2. Closed drainage: Antibiotics mandatory to prevent retained loculi/infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [When the cavity is left open to drain freely, there is no need for antibiotic therapy as well. Antibiotics should be used if the abscess cavity is closed after drainage.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Outline the immediate management steps for suspected Gas Gangrene (C. perfringens).
back:
1. Aggressive surgical debridement
2. High-dose IV Penicillin
3. Circulatory support/Resuscitation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): [Once gas gangrene infection is established, large doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues are required.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What is the optimal timing for prophylactic antibiotic administration?
back: Single-shot IV administration at the induction of anesthesia to ensure peak tissue levels before the first incision.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia is therefore optimal... tissue levels should be present at the time at which the first incision is made.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: List the four diagnostic criteria for Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS).
back:
1. Temp: >38°C or <36°C
2. Heart Rate: >90/min
3. Resp Rate: >20/min
4. WCC: >12 or <4 x 10^9/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [Table 5.3: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C); tachycardia (>90/min); tachypnoea (>20/min); white cell count >12 × 10 9 /litre or <4 × 10 9 /litre]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What prevention strategy is used for heavily contaminated or 'dirty' wounds?
back: Delayed primary closure or secondary closure (waiting for granulation) rather than immediate primary suturing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): [Delayed primary, or secondary, closure remains useful in heavily contaminated wounds.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Outline the management for Synergistic Spreading Gangrene (Necrotizing Fasciitis).
back:
1. Wide excision of necrotic tissue
2. Broad-spectrum antibiotics
3. Aggressive circulatory support
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): [Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy must be combined with aggressive circulatory support. Locally, there should be wide excision of necrotic tissue and laying open of affected areas.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Describe the management for C. difficile-associated pseudomembranous colitis.
back:
1. Stop offending antibiotics (e.g., Quinolones)
2. Fluid resuscitation
3. Oral Metronidazole or Vancomycin
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): [Treatment involves resuscitation and antibiotic therapy with metronidazole or vancomycin.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What is the preferred preoperative hair removal method to reduce SSI risk?
back: Hair clipping (not shaving) immediately before surgery in the operating theatre.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): [Preoperative skin shaving should be undertaken in the operating theatre... hair clipping is best, with the lowest rate of infection.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What is the primary surgical management for a localized abscess?
back:
- Incision and drainage (I&D) of the cavity.
- Curettage of the abscess walls.
- Allow healing by secondary intention if left open.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): Whenever pus was localised in an infected wound, it needed to be drained... Abscess cavities need cleaning out after incision and drainage and are traditionally encouraged to heal by secondary intention.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Explain the 'decisive period' regarding the administration of prophylactic antibiotics.
back:
- A 4-hour window after tissue breach before infection establishes.
- Prophylactics must reach tissues above MIC90 during this specific interval to be effective.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established enough to cause an infection... This interval is called the ‘decisive period’.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Contrast the prevention of SSI regarding preoperative hair removal methods.
back:
- Hair clipping is the preferred method.
- Shaving the night before doubles infection rates due to microscopic skin injuries facilitating colonization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): Preoperative skin shaving... may be doubled if shaving is performed the night before... hair clipping is best, with the lowest rate of infection.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Outline initial management for a patient with suspected necrotizing fasciitis.
back:
- Aggressive circulatory support (resuscitation).
- Immediate wide surgical excision/debridement of all necrotic tissue.
- High-dose intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy must be combined with aggressive circulatory support. Locally, there should be wide excision of necrotic tissue.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: When must prophylactic antibiotics be repeated during a surgical procedure?
back:
- During operations exceeding 4 hours.
- In cases of excessive blood loss.
- If unexpected gross contamination occurs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): In long operations or when there is excessive blood loss, or when unexpected contamination occurs, antibiotics may be repeated at 4-hourly intervals during the surgery.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What defines a major surgical site infection (SSI) requiring intervention?
back:
- Spontaneous discharge of significant pus.
- Necessity for a secondary procedure to drain it.
- Presence of systemic signs (tachycardia, pyrexia).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus spontaneously or needs a secondary procedure to drain it.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: How are heavily contaminated wounds managed to prevent trapped infection?
back:
- Leave the wound open initially.
- Perform delayed primary closure or secondary closure once granulation tissue forms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): Delayed primary, or secondary, closure remains useful in heavily contaminated wounds.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Outline the management of an established gas gangrene infection.
back:
- Aggressive surgical debridement of affected tissues.
- Large doses of intravenous penicillin.
- Circulatory support to manage systemic collapse.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): Once gas gangrene infection is established, large doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues are required.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Why is hand washing mandatory despite the availability of alcoholic gels?
back:
- Alcoholic gels are ineffective against Clostridium difficile spores.
- Physical washing is required to mechanically remove spores in infected environments.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): Alcoholic hand gels... do not destroy the spores of Clostridium difficile, which may cause pseudomembranous colitis.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What are the 'universal precautions' for preventing viral transmission in theatre?
back:
- Full face masks and waterproof gowns.
- Double gloving.
- Passing sharps in a kidney dish (no-touch).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): Universal precautions... full face mask... double gloving... respect is required for sharps, with passage in a kidney dish.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What is the primary surgical management for a localized abscess?
back: - Incision and drainage (I&D) of pus.- Curettage of the abscess walls.- Cavity is typically left open to heal by secondary intention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Whenever pus was localised in an infected wound, it needed to be drained. ... Abscess cavities need cleaning out after incision and drainage and are traditionally encouraged to heal by secondary intention.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Define the 'decisive period' for preventing surgical site infections.
back: - The 4-hour interval after tissue breach before bacterial growth establishes infection.- Prophylactic antibiotics are most effective when tissue levels exceed the MIC during this period.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established enough to cause an infection after a breach in the tissues... This interval is called the ‘decisive period’.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: How should heavily contaminated or dirty wounds be closed to prevent infection?
back: - Avoid immediate primary closure.- Use delayed primary or secondary closure.- This allows for granulation before finalizing the wound edges.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): [Delayed primary, or secondary, closure remains useful in heavily contaminated wounds.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What are the immediate management steps for established Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens)?
back: - Aggressive surgical debridement of necrotic tissue.- Large doses of intravenous penicillin.- Circulatory support to manage systemic collapse.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): [Once gas gangrene infection is established, large doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues are required.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: When should prophylactic antibiotics be repeated intraoperatively?
back: - During long operations (every 4 hours).- In cases of excessive blood loss.- When unexpected major contamination occurs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [In long operations or when there is excessive blood loss, or when unexpected contamination occurs, antibiotics may be repeated at 4-hourly intervals during the surgery.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What are the three core criteria for defining a 'Major' Surgical Site Infection (SSI)?
back: - Significant discharge of pus.- Systemic illness (pyrexia, tachycardia).- Requirement for secondary drainage procedures or delayed home return.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus spontaneously or needs a secondary procedure to drain it. The patient may have systemic signs.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What preoperative hair removal technique is associated with the lowest infection rate?
back: - Hair clipping is the best method.- Avoid shaving the night before, as skin micro-injury enhances bacterial colonization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): [Preoperative skin shaving... may be doubled if shaving is performed the night before... Cream depilation is messy and hair clipping is best, with the lowest rate of infection.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Outline the management of Synergistic Spreading Gangrene (Necrotising Fasciitis).
back: - Aggressive circulatory support.- Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy.- Extensive wide excision (debridement) of necrotic tissue and laying open affected areas.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy must be combined with aggressive circulatory support. Locally, there should be wide excision of necrotic tissue and laying open of affected areas.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What is the prophylactic protocol for Tetanus in an unimmunized patient with a soiled wound?
back: - Three-dose course of Tetanus Toxoid.- Prophylactic Benzylpenicillin.- Consider human immunoglobulin (antitoxin) administration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): [if the patient is not immunised at all, a three-dose course is given together with prophylactic benzylpenicillin... administration of antitoxin using human immunoglobulin ought to be considered.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: List four 'Universal Precautions' for surgeons operating on HIV/Hepatitis patients.
back: - Double gloving.- Protective face mask/spectacles.- Use of waterproof gowns.- Passing sharps in a kidney dish (no hand-to-hand).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): [use of a full face mask... fully waterproof, disposable gowns... double gloving needed... respect is required for sharps, with passage in a kidney dish.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What is the gold standard initial management for a localized surgical abscess?
back:
● Incision and drainage (I&D).
● Cleaning out the cavity.
● Healing by secondary intention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Abscesses need drainage... An open abscess cavity heals by secondary intention.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Explain the significance of the 'decisive period' in prophylactic antibiotic timing.
back:
● 4-hour interval before bacterial growth establishes.
● Antibiotics must exceed MIC90 during contamination.
● Strategies fail after this window.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established enough to cause an infection... This interval is called the ‘decisive period’.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Contrast the requirement for antibiotics in open vs. closed abscess drainage.
back:
● Open cavity: No antibiotics needed if draining freely.
● Closed cavity: Antibiotics are mandatory after drainage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [When the cavity is left open to drain freely, there is no need for antibiotic therapy... Antibiotics should be used if the abscess cavity is closed after drainage.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Initial management steps for a patient with wound crepitus and sweet-smelling exudate?
back:
● Aggressive debridement of necrotic tissue.
● High-dose intravenous penicillin.
● Circulatory support/resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 70 (Book Page)-71: [Once gas gangrene infection is established, large doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues are required.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What are the pharmacological management steps for Clostridium difficile pseudomembranous colitis?
back:
● Fluid resuscitation.
● Oral metronidazole or vancomycin therapy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): [Treatment involves resuscitation and antibiotic therapy with metronidazole or vancomycin.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Identify the most effective preoperative hair removal strategy to prevent SSI.
back:
● Hair clipping (lowest infection rate).
● Avoid shaving night before (doubles SSI risk).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): [Preoperative skin shaving... may be doubled if shaving is performed the night before... hair clipping is best, with the lowest rate of infection.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: How should heavily contaminated or 'dirty' wounds be closed to prevent infection?
back:
● Leave wound open initially.
● Perform delayed primary or secondary closure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): [Delayed primary, or secondary, closure remains useful in heavily contaminated wounds.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Outline the management for Synergistic Spreading Gangrene (e.g., Fournier’s gangrene).
back:
● Aggressive circulatory support.
● Wide excision of necrotic tissue.
● Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy must be combined with aggressive circulatory support... there should be wide excision of necrotic tissue.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Which two perioperative physiological interventions significantly reduce SSI rates during recovery?
back:
● Avoidance of hypothermia.
● Supplemental oxygen administration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): [There is a high level of evidence that both the perioperative avoidance of hypothermia and the use of supplemental oxygen during recovery significantly reduce the rate of SSIs.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What is the optimal timing and route for surgical prophylactic antibiotics?
back:
● Intravenous administration.
● At induction of anesthesia (single-shot).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia is therefore optimal... no evidence that further doses... are of any value.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What is the primary surgical management principle for a localized abscess?
back:
• Incision and drainage.
• Thorough cleaning/curettage of the cavity.
• Healing by secondary intention if left open to drain freely.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): [Whenever pus was localised in an infected wound, it needed to be drained... Abscesses need drainage... An open abscess cavity heals by secondary intention]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Define the 'decisive period' regarding antibiotic prophylaxis in surgical procedures.
back:
• The 4-hour window after tissue breach before bacterial growth is established.
• Antibiotics must be present in tissues above the MIC90 during this time to prevent infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established... This interval is called the ‘decisive period’ and strategies aimed at preventing infection... become ineffective after this time]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: How is a 'major' surgical site infection (SSI) distinguished from a 'minor' one?
back:
• Major SSI: Discharges significant pus, requires secondary drainage, or causes systemic illness (tachycardia/fever).
• Minor SSI: Serous discharge, localized, no systemic signs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [A major SSI is defined as a wound that either discharges significant quantities of pus spontaneously or needs a secondary procedure to drain it. The patient may have systemic signs such as tachycardia, pyrexia]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Outline the immediate management steps for a patient with clinically diagnosed gas gangrene.
back:
• Aggressive surgical debridement of necrotic tissue.
• High-dose intravenous penicillin.
• Intensive circulatory resuscitation and organ support.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): [Once gas gangrene infection is established, large doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues are required... Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy must be combined with aggressive circulatory support.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What is the optimal timing and route for administering prophylactic antibiotics?
back:
• Single-shot intravenous administration.
• Given at the induction of anesthesia to ensure peak tissue levels during initial incision.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia is therefore optimal... Plan for single-shot intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: List the clinical criteria used to define Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS).
back:
Two or more of:
• Temperature >38°C or <36°C.
• Heart Rate >90/min.
• Respiratory Rate >20/min.
• WBC >12,000 or <4,000 cells/μL.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [Table 5.3: SIRS is Two of: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C); tachycardia (>90/min); tachypnoea (>20/min); white cell count >12 × 10 9 /litre or <4 × 10 9 /litre]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Which surgical closure strategy is preferred for heavily contaminated or 'dirty' wounds?
back:
• Delayed primary closure or secondary closure.
• Involves leaving the wound open to granulate before closing later to minimize infection risk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): [Delayed primary, or secondary, closure remains useful in heavily contaminated wounds... Waiting for the wound to granulate and then performing a delayed primary or secondary closure may be considered a better option]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Identify the hallmark signs of Synergistic Spreading Gangrene (Fournier’s/Meleney’s).
back:
• Severe wound pain out of proportion to signs.
• Tissue crepitus and foul smell.
• Widespread subdermal gangrene extending beyond skin erythema.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): [Severe wound pain, signs of spreading inflammation with crepitus and smell are all signs of the infection spreading. Untreated, it will lead to widespread local gangrene... subdermal spread of gangrene is always much more extensive than appears]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Explain the role of bacterial translocation in the development of surgical sepsis.
back:
• Gut failure allows bacteria (Gram-negatives) to move to mesenteric nodes.
• Endotoxins stimulate macrophage release of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNFα).
• This triggers a systemic inflammatory response (SIRS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [bacteria... translocate to the mesenteric nodes and cause the release of endotoxins... stimulate the release of cytokines from macrophages... leading to either cellulitis, lymphangitis, abscess formation or bacteraemia.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: What is the most effective preoperative hair removal method for preventing SSI?
back:
• Hair clipping immediately before surgery.
• Razors/shaving are avoided as micro-injuries facilitate bacterial colonization and double infection rates.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): [Preoperative skin shaving... SSI rate... doubled if shaving is performed the night before... hair clipping is best, with the lowest rate of infection.]

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What is the definitive management for a localized surgical abscess?
back:
- Incision and drainage (I&D).
- Cleaning/curettage of the cavity.
- Healing by secondary intention (unless primarily closed under antibiotic cover).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): Abscesses need drainage... When the cavity is left open to drain freely, there is no need for antibiotic therapy as well... An open abscess cavity heals by secondary intention.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Define the 'decisive period' in surgical infection prevention.
back:
- A 4-hour window after tissue injury before bacterial growth establishes infection.
- Prophylactic antibiotics must achieve MIC90 in tissues during this window to be effective.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established enough to cause an infection... This interval is called the ‘decisive period’.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Contrast the efficacy of hair clipping versus shaving for SSI prevention.
back:
- Hair clipping: Lowest infection rate.
- Shaving (night before): Doubles infection rate due to micro-trauma/bacterial colonisation.
- Timing: Should be done immediately before surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): SSI rate after clean wound surgery may be doubled if shaving is performed the night before... hair clipping is best, with the lowest rate of infection.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Outline the immediate management of Gas Gangrene (C. perfringens).
back:
1. Aggressive surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue.
2. High-dose intravenous Penicillin.
3. Aggressive circulatory support (resuscitation).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 71 (Book Page): Once gas gangrene infection is established, large doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues are required.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: What is the optimal pharmacological strategy for surgical antibiotic prophylaxis?
back:
- Single-shot IV administration at induction of anesthesia.
- Repeat only during long operations (>4 hours) or excessive blood loss.
- No evidence for continuing doses postoperatively.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Plan for single-shot intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia. Repeat only during long operations or if there is excessive blood loss.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: List the clinical criteria for Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS).
back:
Two or more of:
- Temp: >38°C or <36°C.
- HR: >90/min.
- RR: >20/min.
- WBC: >12,000 or <4,000/mm³.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): SIRS is Two of: hyperthermia (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C); tachycardia (>90/min...); tachypnoea (>20/min); white cell count >12 or <4.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: When should delayed primary or secondary closure be utilized?
back:
- Indicated for heavily contaminated or dirty wounds (e.g., faecal peritonitis).
- Prevents SSI by allowing granulation before closure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): Delayed primary, or secondary, closure remains useful in heavily contaminated wounds.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Describe the surgical management strategy for Necrotizing Fasciitis.
back:
- Aggressive, wide excision of all necrotic tissue (laying open affected areas).
- Broad-spectrum antibiotics.
- Intensive circulatory support; subsequent skin grafting often required.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): Locally, there should be wide excision of necrotic tissue and laying open of affected areas... combined with aggressive circulatory support.

category: Outline steps of initial management and prevention strategies
front: Q: Explain the role of gut translocation in postoperative SIRS.
back:
- Starvation/sepsis causes breakdown of gut barrier.
- Gram-negative bacilli translocate to mesenteric nodes.
- Release of endotoxin (LPS) triggers cytokine-mediated systemic inflammation.
