citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): [Staphylococcus epidermidis... is now recognised as a major threat in vascular and orthopaedic prosthetic surgery... The bacteria form biofilms which adhere to prosthetic surfaces.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the optimal timing for the administration of prophylactic antibiotics in surgery?
back:
● At induction of anesthesia
● Must ensure peak tissue levels before the first incision
● Administered within the 'decisive period'
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia is therefore optimal, as unexpected delays in the timing of surgery may occur before then and antibiotic tissue levels may fall off before the surgery starts.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Define the 'decisive period' in the context of surgical wound infection.
back:
● The 4-hour interval after tissue breach
● Window before bacterial growth becomes established
● Prophylaxis is ineffective after this period
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [This interval is called the ‘decisive period’ and strategies aimed at preventing infection from taking a hold become ineffective after this time period.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What determines the 'choice' of antibiotic for surgical prophylaxis?
back:
● Expected spectrum of pathogens for the specific site
● Type of surgery
● Local hospital guidelines and patient allergies
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [The choice of an antibiotic depends on the expected spectrum of organisms likely to be encountered, which will depend on the site and type of surgery...]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Under which two conditions should a prophylactic antibiotic dose be repeated intraoperatively?
back:
● Operations exceeding 4 hours in duration
● Excessive blood loss during the procedure
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [In long operations or when there is excessive blood loss... antibiotics may be repeated at 4-hourly intervals during the surgery.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the recommended duration of antibiotic prophylaxis for most surgical procedures?
back:
● Single-shot (single dose) intravenous administration
● No evidence of benefit for doses continued after surgery
● Prolonged use encourages bacterial resistance
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: When is antibiotic prophylaxis indicated for 'Clean' (Type I) surgical wounds?
back:
● Only if a prosthetic implant is being used
● When infection would lead to catastrophic results
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [The value of antibiotic prophylaxis is low in non-prosthetic clean surgery... The exception to this is where a prosthetic implant is used, as the results of infection are so catastrophic.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Scenario: A patient with a heart valve prosthesis undergoes dental surgery. What is the prophylactic requirement?
back:
● Prophylactic antibiotics are mandatory
● Aim: Prevent bacterial colonisation of the prosthesis during transient bacteraemia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Patients with known valvular disease of the heart (or with any implanted vascular or orthopaedic prosthesis) should have prophylactic antibiotics during dental, urological or open viscus surgery...]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: How does the antibiotic strategy change for 'Dirty' wounds compared to standard prophylaxis?
back:
● Shifts from prophylaxis to 'therapeutic' treatment
● Duration: Typically a 5-day course of therapeutic antibiotics
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [When wounds are heavily contaminated or when an incision is made into an abscess, a 5-day course of therapeutic antibiotics may be justified... treatment is needed rather than prophylaxis.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What target tissue level must a prophylactic antibiotic achieve to be effective?
back:
● Above the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC90) for expected pathogens
● Maintained throughout the entire duration of contamination risk
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [The tissue levels of antibiotics during the period when bacterial contamination is likely to occur should be above the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC 90) for the expected pathogens.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: List the two classifications of surgery where antibiotic prophylaxis is most clearly proven effective.
back:
● Clean-contaminated operations
● Contaminated operations
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [There is undisputed evidence that prophylactic antibiotics are effective in reducing the risk of infection in clean-contaminated and contaminated operations.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: At what specific surgical stage should prophylactic antibiotics be administered to ensure maximal tissue levels?
back: Intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia, before the first incision is made and contamination occurs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia is therefore optimal, as unexpected delays in the timing of surgery may occur before then and antibiotic tissue levels may fall off before the surgery starts.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the 'decisive period' regarding antibiotic prophylaxis in surgical infections?
back: The four-hour interval after tissue breach before bacterial growth becomes established and infection takes hold.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [There is up to a 4-hour interval before bacterial growth becomes established enough to cause an infection after a breach in the tissues... This interval is called the ‘decisive period’.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: In which specific type of 'Clean' surgery is antibiotic prophylaxis mandatory?
back: When a prosthetic implant is used, due to the catastrophic consequences of potential infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [The exception to this is where a prosthetic implant is used, as the results of infection are so catastrophic that even a small risk of infection is unacceptable.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Under what two intraoperative conditions should a dose of prophylactic antibiotic be repeated?
back:
1. Long operations (exceeding 4-hour intervals).
2. Excessive blood loss during the procedure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [In long operations or when there is excessive blood loss, or when unexpected contamination occurs, antibiotics may be repeated at 4-hourly intervals during the surgery.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What defines the required tissue concentration of a prophylactic antibiotic during surgery?
back: Levels must remain above the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC 90) for the expected pathogens.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [The tissue levels of antibiotics during the period when bacterial contamination is likely to occur should be above the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC 90) for the expected pathogens.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: How does the antibiotic strategy change for 'Dirty' wounds compared to standard prophylaxis?
back: A 5-day therapeutic course is justified because the wound is assumed to be inevitably infected.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [When wounds are heavily contaminated or when an incision is made into an abscess, a 5-day course of therapeutic antibiotics may be justified on the assumption that the wound is inevitably infected.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Why are prophylactic antibiotics generally discouraged in elective clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: Low infection rates mean the value is minimal, and use encourages the emergence of resistant strains.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [The value of antibiotic prophylaxis is low in non-prosthetic clean surgery, with most trials showing no clear benefit... indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What three factors primarily determine the specific choice of antibiotic for surgical prophylaxis?
back:
1. Expected organism spectrum at the site.
2. Local hospital standardized policies.
3. Patient antibiotic allergies.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [The choice of an antibiotic depends on the expected spectrum of organisms likely to be encountered, which will depend on the site and type of surgery and whether or not the patient has any antibiotic allergies.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: For which non-viscus procedures do patients with heart valve disease require antibiotic prophylaxis?
back: Dental work and urethral instrumentation (to prevent colonization during transient bacteraemia).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Patients with known valvular disease... should have prophylactic antibiotics during dental, urological or open viscus surgery, to prevent bacterial colonisation of the valve... during the transient bacteraemia.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the recommended duration of antibiotic doses after surgery for standard prophylaxis?
back: None; evidence shows additional postoperative doses provide no value and promote resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: When is the optimal time to administer prophylactic antibiotics for peak tissue levels during surgical incision?
back: A: Intravenously at the induction of anesthesia to ensure maximal levels before the first incision is made.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia is therefore optimal, as unexpected delays in the timing of surgery may occur before then and antibiotic tissue levels may fall off before the surgery starts.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the 'decisive period' in surgical infection pathophysiology?
back: A: The 4-hour window after tissue breach during which prophylaxis is effective before bacterial growth becomes established.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): This interval is called the ‘decisive period’ and strategies aimed at preventing infection from taking a hold become ineffective after this time period.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the standard recommended duration for prophylactic antibiotic administration in elective surgery?
back: A: A single-shot intravenous dose; there is no evidence that further doses after surgery provide any value.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: In which two specific scenarios should prophylactic antibiotics be repeated during a single operation?
back:
1. Long operations (at 4-hourly intervals).
2. Excessive blood loss.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): In long operations or when there is excessive blood loss, or when unexpected contamination occurs, antibiotics may be repeated at 4-hourly intervals during the surgery.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What defines the 'choice' of a prophylactic antibiotic according to surgical principles?
back: A: It depends on the expected spectrum of organisms for that specific site and the patient's allergy history.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): The choice of an antibiotic depends on the expected spectrum of organisms likely to be encountered, which will depend on the site and type of surgery and whether or not the patient has any antibiotic allergies.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: When is antibiotic prophylaxis indicated for 'clean' non-prosthetic surgery?
back: A: Generally not indicated because infection rates are low (<2%), and it may encourage bacterial resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): The use of prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery is of less value as infection rates are low and the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Why are prosthetic implants an absolute indication for prophylaxis even in clean surgery?
back: A: Because the consequences of infection (prosthetic failure/catastrophic illness) outweigh the low risk of surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): The exception to this is where a prosthetic implant is used, as the results of infection are so catastrophic that even a small risk of infection is unacceptable.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Contrast the antibiotic management of a 'contaminated' vs. a 'dirty' wound (e.g., abscess incision).
back: A: Contaminated wounds receive prophylaxis; dirty wounds receive a 5-day therapeutic course as they are considered already infected.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): When wounds are heavily contaminated or when an incision is made into an abscess, a 5-day course of therapeutic antibiotics may be justified on the assumption that the wound is inevitably infected.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Why must antibiotic tissue levels stay above the MIC90 during a prolonged operation?
back: A: Because tissue levels fall faster than serum levels, leaving the wound vulnerable to contamination despite circulating drug.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): In long operations... antibiotics may be repeated at 4-hourly intervals during the surgery, because tissue antibiotic levels often fall faster than serum levels.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Which patients require prophylaxis during dental or urological surgery to prevent prosthetic infection?
back: A: Patients with known heart valve disease or any implanted vascular/orthopedic prosthesis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Patients with known valvular disease of the heart (or with any implanted vascular or orthopaedic prosthesis) should have prophylactic antibiotics during dental, urological or open viscus surgery.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary consequence of indiscriminate antibiotic use in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: It encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria with minimal benefit to the low baseline infection rate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiology of antibiotic-induced pseudomembranous colitis.
back: Antibiotics destroy normal colonic flora, allowing an overgrowth of the commensal Clostridium difficile to pathological, toxin-producing levels.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora by antibiotic therapy allows an overgrowth of the normal gut commensal C. diff to pathological levels.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What clinical entity forms when an undrained abscess is partly sterilized by antibiotics?
back: An antibioma (a firm, sterile inflammatory mass that mimics a tumor).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): If it is partly sterilised with antibiotics, an antibioma may form.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: A 70-year-old patient develops severe diarrhea after Ciprofloxacin therapy. What is the most likely complication?
back: Pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile overgrowth); quinolones are identified as highest risk in elderly or immunocompromised patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): quinolones such as ciprofloxacin seem to be the highest risk, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: By what specific biochemical mechanism do many Staphylococci become resistant to penicillin?
back: Acquisition of beta-lactamases, which enzymatically break the beta-lactam ring of the antibiotic.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): Often bacteria develop resistance through the acquisition of b -lactamases, which break up the b -lactam ring present in the molecular structure of many antibiotics.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What are the risks associated with Extended Spectrum Beta-Lactamases (ESBLs) in gram-negative bacilli?
back: They confer resistance to most cephalosporins and make finding effective treatment for infections like UTIs difficult.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): development of extended spectrum b -lactamases (ESBLs) in many of this group of bacteria, which confer resistance to many antibiotics, particularly cephalosporins.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is providing repeated antibiotic doses after the 'decisive period' discouraged in surgical prophylaxis?
back: Postoperative doses have no proven value in preventing infection and solely encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value... the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: A patient on prolonged, broad-spectrum antibiotics develops a new fever. Which specific pathogen type should be suspected?
back: Opportunistic fungal infection (e.g., Candida).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): Opportunistic infection with fungi is an example, particularly when prolonged and changing antibiotic regimes have been used.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the risk of frequent empirical antibiotic changes in a patient with a poor clinical response?
back: It promotes antibiotic resistance and increases the risk of complications such as C. difficile enteritis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): change of antibiotics promotes resistance and risks complications, such as C. difficile enteritis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of failing to provide antibiotic cover for dental work in a patient with a prosthetic heart valve?
back: Bacterial colonization of the prosthesis due to transient bacteraemia, leading to prosthetic endocarditis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Patients with known valvular disease... should have prophylactic antibiotics during dental... surgery, to prevent bacterial colonisation of the valve... during the transient bacteraemia.

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the 'decisive period' in surgical antibiotic prophylaxis?
back: The interval (up to 4 hours) before bacterial growth becomes established after tissue breach; prophylaxis is ineffective after this window.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): [This interval is called the ‘decisive period’ and strategies aimed at preventing infection from taking a hold become ineffective after this time period.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Why are prophylactic antibiotics ideally administered at the induction of anesthesia?
back: To ensure maximal tissue levels exceed the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC90) before the first incision is made.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Ideally, maximal blood and tissue levels should be present at the time at which the first incision is made and before contamination occurs. ...Intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia is therefore optimal]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: On what basis is the specific antibiotic chosen for surgical prophylaxis?
back: The expected spectrum of pathogens likely to be encountered at the specific surgical site and the procedure type.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [The choice of an antibiotic depends on the expected spectrum of organisms likely to be encountered, which will depend on the site and type of surgery]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the standard recommended duration for surgical antibiotic prophylaxis?
back: A single-shot intravenous dose at induction. Further postoperative doses are not indicated and increase the risk of resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Plan for single-shot intravenous administration at induction of anaesthesia ... There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: When should a prophylactic antibiotic dose be repeated during a surgical procedure?
back:
1. During long operations (4-hourly intervals)
2. Excessive blood loss
3. Unexpected contamination
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [In long operations or when there is excessive blood loss, or when unexpected contamination occurs, antibiotics may be repeated at 4-hourly intervals during the surgery]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Why is prophylaxis mandatory in 'clean' surgery if a prosthetic implant is used?
back: While infection rates are low, the consequences of infection in prosthetic surgery are catastrophic, making any risk unacceptable.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [The exception to this is where a prosthetic implant is used, as the results of infection are so catastrophic that even a small risk of infection is unacceptable.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Which wound classifications have 'undisputed evidence' for antibiotic prophylaxis benefit?
back: Clean-contaminated and contaminated operations. Benefit is low in clean, non-prosthetic surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [There is undisputed evidence that prophylactic antibiotics are effective in reducing the risk of infection in clean-contaminated and contaminated operations.]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the recommended antibiotic duration for 'dirty' wounds (e.g., perforated viscus)?
back: A 5-day therapeutic course is justified as the wound is considered already infected rather than just contaminated.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [When wounds are heavily contaminated ... a 5-day course of therapeutic antibiotics may be justified on the assumption that the wound is inevitably infected]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: Why do patients with heart valve disease require prophylaxis for dental or urological work?
back: To prevent bacterial colonization of the valve during the transient bacteraemia caused by instrumentation or visceral surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [Patients with known valvular disease of the heart ... should have prophylactic antibiotics during dental, urological or open viscus surgery, to prevent bacterial colonisation of the valve]

category: Explain the principles of timing, choice, and duration of prophylaxis
front: Q: What is the primary clinical risk of continuing antibiotic prophylaxis beyond the surgery?
back: It encourages the emergence of resistant bacterial strains without providing additional protection against surgical site infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis ... and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What was the historical consequence of the 'laudable pus' misunderstanding in wound management?
back: Practitioners inappropriately applied noxious substances like feces to wounds, erroneously believing healing required active pus formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 63 (Book Page): Until well into the Middle Ages, some practitioners promoted suppuration in wounds by the application of noxious substances, including faeces, in the misguided belief that healing could not occur without pus formation.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: How do bacteria most commonly acquire resistance to β-lactam antibiotics?
back: Through the acquisition of β-lactamases or extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) which enzymatically break the antibiotic's β-lactam ring.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): Often bacteria develop resistance through the acquisition of b -lactamases, which break up the b -lactam ring present in the molecular structure of many antibiotics.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary risk of using prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: It provides minimal clinical value while actively encouraging the emergence of resistant bacterial strains.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): The use of prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery is of less value as infection rates are low and the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Explain the consequence of broad-spectrum antibiotic use on colonic flora leading to colitis.
back: Destruction of normal bacterial flora allows the overgrowth of Clostridium difficile to pathological, toxin-producing levels.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page)-66: Clostridium difficile is the cause of pseudomembranous colitis, where destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora by antibiotic therapy allows an overgrowth of the normal gut commensal C. diff to pathological levels.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is antibiotic prophylaxis ineffective if administered after the 'decisive period'?
back: Bacterial growth becomes established roughly 4 hours after tissue breach, making preventive strategies futile once the infection takes hold.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): strategies aimed at preventing infection from taking a hold become ineffective after this time period [the 4-hour decisive period].

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the specific complication of using silk sutures for skin closure?
back: Silk reduces the critical inoculum of bacteria needed for infection, leading to the formation of suture abscesses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): If there is a silk suture in tissue, the critical number of organisms needed to start an infection is reduced logarithmically. Silk should not be used to close skin as it causes suture abscesses...

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What clinical entity is formed when an abscess is inappropriately treated with antibiotics alone?
back: An antibioma; this is a mass resulting from the partial sterilization of a localized infection without surgical drainage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): If it is partly sterilised with antibiotics, an antibioma may form.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of continuing prophylactic antibiotics beyond the immediate postoperative period?
back: It offers no proven benefit in preventing SSI and specifically promotes the development of antibiotic resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: In severe sepsis, what happens to the host's resistance as more organs fail?
back: Resistance is further reduced, creating a 'vicious cycle' where organ dysfunction (MODS) increasingly leads to certain death (MSOF).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): In this state, the body’s resistance to infection is reduced and a vicious cycle develops where the more organs that fail, the more likely it becomes that death will follow...

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What was the consequence of failing to implement Semmelweis's hand-washing protocols?
back: Puerperal sepsis rates remained above 10%, which could have been reduced to under 2% with basic hygiene.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): Ignac Semmelweis showed that puerperal sepsis could be reduced from over 10% to under 2% by the simple act of hand washing... He was ignored by his contemporaries...

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary consequence of using antibiotics indiscriminately in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: It encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria, as the value of prophylaxis is low when baseline infection rates are already minimal.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Pathophysiologically, why does inappropriate antibiotic therapy lead to Pseudomembranous colitis?
back: Destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora allows an overgrowth of the commensal Clostridium difficile to pathological levels.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): Clostridium difficile is the cause of pseudomembranous colitis, where destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora by antibiotic therapy allows an overgrowth of the normal gut commensal C. diff to pathological levels.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Which specific antibiotic class poses the highest risk for C. difficile overgrowth in elderly or immunocompromised patients?
back: Quinolones, such as ciprofloxacin.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): Any antibiotic may cause this phenomenon, although the quinolones such as ciprofloxacin seem to be the highest risk, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: A surgeon leaves a pool of alcohol-based antiseptic on a patient's skin before using diathermy. What is the likely complication?
back: The fluid may ignite with the diathermy, causing a surgical burn on the patient.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): caution should be taken not to leave a pool of alcohol-based fluid on the skin which could ignite with diathermy and burn the patient.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is it considered inappropriate to continue prophylactic antibiotics after the surgical procedure has ended?
back:
1. No evidence of value in further infection prevention.
2. Encourages the development of antibiotic resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 75 (Book Page): There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the iatrogenic consequence of using silk for skin closure?
back: It causes suture abscesses because the material logarithmically reduces the critical number of organisms required to initiate an infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): If there is a silk suture in tissue, the critical number of organisms needed to start an infection is reduced logarithmically. Silk should not be used to close skin as it causes suture abscesses for this reason.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of performing preoperative skin shaving the night before a clean surgery?
back: The SSI rate may be doubled due to minor skin injuries that enhance superficial bacterial colonization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): the SSI rate after clean wound surgery may be doubled if shaving is performed the night before, because minor skin injury enhances superficial bacterial colonisation.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is the frequent, unjustified change of empirical antibiotic regimes considered dangerous in surgical wards?
back:
1. Promotes bacterial resistance.
2. Increases the risk of C. difficile enteritis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 75 (Book Page): change of antibiotics promotes resistance and risks complications, such as C. difficile enteritis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: How do prolonged or frequently changing antibiotic regimes lead to opportunistic fungal infections?
back: By creating an environment of reduced host resistance where non-pathogenic organisms (like fungi) begin to act as pathogens.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): Opportunistic infection with fungi is an example, particularly when prolonged and changing antibiotic regimes have been used.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the risk of omitting prophylactic antibiotics in contaminated surgery (e.g., open viscus with spillage)?
back: The infection rate rises from approximately 6% (with prophylaxis) to 13-20% (without).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 75 (Book Page): Table 5.4: Contaminated (open viscus with spillage...) Infection rate with prophylaxis (%) 6. Infection rate without prophylaxis (%) 13–20.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of using prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: It is of little value and encourages the emergence of resistant bacterial strains.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is skin shaving the night before surgery considered inappropriate?
back: It can double the SSI rate by causing minor skin injuries that enhance bacterial colonization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): the SSI rate after clean wound surgery may be doubled if shaving is performed the night before, because minor skin injury enhances superficial bacterial colonisation.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the risk of continuing prophylactic antibiotics beyond the immediate postoperative period?
back: It provides no additional benefit and promotes the development of antibiotic resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: A patient on ciprofloxacin develops severe colitis. Which pathogen is most likely responsible?
back: Clostridium difficile (C. diff). Quinolones carry the highest risk for this overgrowth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): Any antibiotic may cause this phenomenon, although the quinolones such as ciprofloxacin seem to be the highest risk, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the surgical consequence of using silk for skin closure?
back: It causes suture abscesses because it reduces the critical number of organisms needed to initiate infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): If there is a silk suture in tissue, the critical number of organisms needed to start an infection is reduced logarithmically. Silk should not be used to close skin as it causes suture abscesses for this reason.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why are alcoholic hand gels inappropriate for managing a ward with Clostridium difficile?
back: Alcoholic hand gels do not destroy Clostridium difficile spores.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): Alcoholic hand gels can act as a substitute for hand washing, but do not destroy the spores of Clostridium difficile, which may cause pseudomembranous colitis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What physical danger arises from leaving excess alcohol-based antiseptic on the skin during surgery?
back: It can ignite with the use of diathermy, resulting in patient burns.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): caution should be taken not to leave a pool of alcohol-based fluid on the skin which could ignite with diathermy and burn the patient.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: How does a prolonged preoperative hospital stay inappropriately affect the risk of infection?
back: It increases the risk of the patient acquiring MRSA and other antibiotic-resistant organisms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): A short preoperative hospital stay lowers the risk of acquiring MRSA, multiply resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci (MRCNS) and other antibiotic-resistant organisms from the hospital environment.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is antibiotic prophylaxis ineffective if given more than 4 hours after tissue breach?
back: The 'decisive period' (first 4 hours) has passed, and bacterial growth has already become established.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): This interval is called the ‘decisive period’ and strategies aimed at preventing infection from taking a hold become ineffective after this time period.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary risk of frequently changing empirical antibiotics without culture-proven indication?
back: It promotes antibiotic resistance and increases the risk of C. difficile enteritis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): such changes are unusual if the empirical choice of antibiotics is sensible; change of antibiotics promotes resistance and risks complications, such as C. difficile enteritis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary consequence of using antibiotics indiscriminately in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: It encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria, providing little benefit as baseline infection rates are already low.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page)-65: [The use of prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery is of less value as infection rates are low and the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: How does inappropriate antibiotic therapy lead to the development of pseudomembranous colitis?
back: It causes destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora, allowing Clostridium difficile to overgrow to pathological levels.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page)-66: [destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora by antibiotic therapy allows an overgrowth of the normal gut commensal C. diff to pathological levels.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Which antibiotic class poses the highest risk for C. difficile overgrowth, particularly in elderly patients?
back: Quinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin) are associated with the highest risk for triggering pseudomembranous colitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): [the quinolones such as ciprofloxacin seem to be the highest risk, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of extending antibiotic prophylaxis into the postoperative period without indication?
back: It provides no evidence-based value in preventing infection and directly encourages the development of antibiotic resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What type of infection is specifically associated with the inappropriate use of prolonged or changing antibiotic regimes?
back: Opportunistic infections, specifically those caused by fungi.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): [Opportunistic infection with fungi is an example, particularly when prolonged and changing antibiotic regimes have been used.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Identify two specific multidrug-resistant pathogens resulting from rising antibiotic resistance in general surgical practice.
back: 1. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). 2. Glycopeptide-resistant enterococci (GRE).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): [there is increasing concern about the rising resistance... in particular the emergence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and glycopeptide-resistant enterococci (GRE).]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Molecularly, how do staphylococci acquire resistance to penicillin after exposure?
back: Through the acquisition of ̢̢-lactamases, enzymes that break the ̢̢-lactam ring in the antibiotic's structure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): [Often bacteria develop resistance through the acquisition of b-lactamases, which break up the b-lactam ring present in the molecular structure of many antibiotics.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary clinical concern regarding the emergence of Extended Spectrum ̢̢-lactamases (ESBLs) in Gram-negative organisms?
back: Significant difficulty in finding effective antibiotics, particularly when treating urinary tract infections caused by these organisms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): [The acquisition of extended spectrum b-lactamases (ESBLs) is an increasing concern in some gram-negative organisms... because it is difficult to find an antibiotic effective against them.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What are the two main risks of frequently and illogically changing empirical antibiotic selections?
back: 1. Promotion of bacterial resistance. 2. Increased risk of complications like C. difficile enteritis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): [change of antibiotics promotes resistance and risks complications, such as C. difficile enteritis.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is antibiotic prophylaxis discouraged in clean surgery where no prosthesis is implanted?
back: Low baseline infection rates make the risk of encouraging resistant strains far outweigh the benefits of use.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page)-65: [The use of prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery is of less value as infection rates are low and the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains.]

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary consequence of the indiscriminate use of antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: It encourages the emergence of resistant bacterial strains with little to no benefit in reducing already low infection rates.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: How do Staphylococci develop biochemical resistance to penicillin?
back: They acquire ̢̢β-lactamases, which are enzymes that break up the ̢̢β-lactam ring in the antibiotic's molecular structure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): Often bacteria develop resistance through the acquisition of b-lactamases, which break up the b-lactam ring present in the molecular structure of many antibiotics.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the pathophysiological cause of pseudomembranous colitis during antibiotic therapy?
back: Destruction of normal colonic bacterial flora allows the overgrowth of the commensal Clostridium difficile to pathological levels.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): Clostridium difficile is the cause of pseudomembranous colitis, where destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora by antibiotic therapy allows an overgrowth of the normal gut commensal C. diff to pathological levels.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: An elderly patient develops toxic megacolon after ciprofloxacin therapy for a minor UTI. Identify the likely complication.
back: Pseudomembranous colitis caused by C. difficile overgrowth; quinolones like ciprofloxacin pose the highest risk in the elderly.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): Any antibiotic may cause this phenomenon, although the quinolones such as ciprofloxacin seem to be the highest risk, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients. In its most severe form, the colitis may lead to perforation.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What clinical entity is formed when a wound abscess is only partially sterilized with antibiotics?
back: An antibioma; this is a sterile, persistent inflammatory mass that fails to fully resolve because the abscess was not drained.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): If it is partly sterilised with antibiotics, an antibioma may form.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the specific resistance concern regarding Extended Spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) in gram-negative bacilli?
back: ESBLs confer resistance to a wide spectrum of antibiotics, making them particularly difficult to treat, especially against cephalosporins.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): Extended spectrum b-lactamases (ESBLs) in many of this group of bacteria, which confer resistance to many antibiotics, particularly cephalosporins.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Apply the principle of the 'decisive period' to justify stopping antibiotics after a single preoperative dose.
back: Antibiotics must be present during the 4-hour 'decisive period' of contamination; further doses post-surgery offer no benefit and encourage resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: A patient on prolonged multi-drug antibiotic therapy develops a white oral coating and systemic deterioration. Explain the mechanism.
back: Opportunistic fungal infection resulting from the suppression of normal protective bacterial flora by prolonged and changing antibiotic regimes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): Opportunistic infection with fungi is an example, particularly when prolonged and changing antibiotic regimes have been used.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is the frequent, empirical change of antibiotics without clinical response discouraged in surgical patients?
back: Frequent changes promote bacterial resistance and significantly increase the risk of severe complications like C. difficile enteritis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): change of antibiotics promotes resistance and risks complications, such as C. difficile enteritis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: How do previously sensitive bacteria acquire resistance traits from other organisms?
back: Resistance can be acquired and shared through the horizontal transfer of plasmids between bacteria.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): Resistance to antibiotics can be acquired by previously sensitive bacteria by transfer through plasmids.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the clinical consequence of an unnecessarily long preoperative hospital stay?
back:
- Increased risk of acquiring MRSA
- Acquisition of multiply resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci (MRCNS)
- Colonization with hospital-acquired antibiotic-resistant organisms
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): A short preoperative hospital stay lowers the risk of acquiring MRSA, multiply resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci (MRCNS) and other antibiotic-resistant organisms from the hospital environment.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is reliance on alcoholic hand gels alone inappropriate for hand hygiene in wards?
back:
- They do not destroy Clostridium difficile spores
- Risk of pseudomembranous colitis outbreak
- Failure to eliminate resistant gut flora in immunocompromised patients
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Alcoholic hand gels can act as a substitute for hand washing, but do not destroy the spores of Clostridium difficile, which may cause pseudomembranous colitis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the infectious consequence of shaving the operative site the night before surgery?
back:
- SSI rate may be doubled
- Minor skin injuries enhance superficial bacterial colonization
- Clipping immediately before surgery is the safer alternative
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Preoperative skin shaving should be undertaken in the operating theatre immediately before surgery as the SSI rate after clean wound surgery may be doubled if shaving is performed the night before.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What complication arises from the use of silk sutures for skin closure?
back:
- Development of suture abscesses
- Silk logarithmically reduces the critical number of organisms needed to initiate infection
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): If there is a silk suture in tissue, the critical number of organisms needed to start an infection is reduced logarithmically. Silk should not be used to close skin as it causes suture abscesses for this reason.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of prolonged and frequently changing antibiotic regimes in surgical patients?
back:
- Development of opportunistic fungal infections
- Emergence of organisms that are normally non-pathogenic
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): In the circumstances of reduced host resistance... microorganisms that are not normally pathogenic may start to behave as pathogens. This is known as opportunistic infection. Opportunistic infection with fungi is an example, particularly when prolonged and changing antibiotic regimes have been used.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is the acquisition of Extended Spectrum Beta-Lactamases (ESBLs) in gram-negative organisms clinically critical?
back:
- Confers resistance to most antibiotics (especially cephalosporins)
- Extreme difficulty in finding an effective antibiotic agent
- Major concern in surgical urinary tract infections
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): The acquisition of extended spectrum b-lactamases (ESBLs) is an increasing concern in some gram-negative organisms... because it is difficult to find an antibiotic effective against them.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What happens if an empirical antibiotic choice is changed frequently without sensitivity evidence?
back:
- Promotes antibiotic resistance
- Increases the risk of Clostridium difficile enteritis
- Indiscriminate use encourages emergence of resistant strains
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): It is illogical to withhold antibiotics until results are available... change of antibiotics promotes resistance and risks complications, such as C. difficile enteritis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of failing to provide a single-shot antibiotic at induction in clean-contaminated surgery?
back:
- SSI rates rise from 3% to 6-9%
- Inadequate tissue levels during the 'decisive period'
- Higher risk of post-operative suppuration
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): Clean-contaminated (viscus opened, minimal spillage): Infection rate with prophylaxis 3%; Infection rate without prophylaxis 6–9%.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Identify the surgical outcome of failing to manage dead space or haematoma during closure.
back:
- Increased risk of wound infection
- Provides a medium for bacterial growth
- Compromises local host response
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): Devitalised tissue, excessive dead space or haematoma, all the results of poor surgical technique, increase the chances of infection.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What does an outbreak of wound infections with identical sensitivity profiles on a ward indicate?
back:
- Exogenous source of infection (staff or environment)
- Requires immediate swabbing of staff and surfaces
- May necessitate temporary ward closure and deep cleaning
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): An outbreak of wound infections on the ward with bacteria having the same antibiotic sensitivity profile implies an exogenous source of infection, which needs to be investigated by swabbing all staff and work surfaces.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary consequence of using prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: The indiscriminate use encourages the emergence of resistant bacterial strains, as infection rates are already low.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological consequence of broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy on the colon.
back: Destruction of normal colonic flora allows overgrowth of C. difficile to pathological levels, causing pseudomembranous colitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora by antibiotic therapy allows an overgrowth of the normal gut commensal C. diff to pathological levels.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the outcome of partially treating an undrained abscess with antibiotics?
back: Formation of an antibioma (a sterilized or partially sterilized mass).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 69 (Book Page): If it is partly sterilised with antibiotics, an antibioma may form.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: An elderly patient on ciprofloxacin develops severe diarrhea and abdominal perforation. Explain the likely mechanism.
back: Antibiotic-associated (C. difficile) colitis; quinolones carry high risk for flora destruction leading to perforation and mortality.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): any antibiotic may cause this phenomenon, although the quinolones such as ciprofloxacin seem to be the highest risk... colitis may lead to perforation.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of continuing prophylactic antibiotics beyond the immediate postoperative period?
back: No clinical benefit is achieved; the practice only encourages the development of antibiotic resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value... the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the diagnostic consequence of prolonged and frequently changing antibiotic regimes?
back: Emergence of opportunistic infections, most commonly fungal infections.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): Opportunistic infection with fungi is an example, particularly when prolonged and changing antibiotic regimes have been used.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is the use of silk suture for skin closure inappropriate regarding infection risk?
back: It causes suture abscesses by logarithmically reducing the critical number of organisms needed to initiate infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): If there is a silk suture in tissue, the critical number of organisms needed to start an infection is reduced logarithmically. Silk should not be used to close skin as it causes suture abscesses.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: A patient shows poor response to empirical antibiotics. What is the risk of an illogical change in therapy?
back: Promotes bacterial resistance and increases the risk of complications like C. difficile enteritis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): change of antibiotics promotes resistance and risks complications, such as C. difficile enteritis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What happens if prophylactic antibiotics are administered after the 'decisive period' (4 hours post-injury)?
back: Strategies to prevent infection become ineffective once bacterial growth is established.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): strategies aimed at preventing infection from taking a hold become ineffective after this time period [the decisive period].

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of relying solely on alcoholic hand gels for C. difficile infection control?
back: Failure to destroy C. difficile spores, leading to continued hospital-acquired transmission.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 73 (Book Page): Alcoholic hand gels... do not destroy the spores of Clostridium difficile, which may cause pseudomembranous colitis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary consequence of indiscriminate antibiotic use in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: It encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria without offering significant clinical benefit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): The use of prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery is of less value as infection rates are low and the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Which specific antibiotic class poses the highest risk for developing C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis?
back: Quinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin), particularly in elderly or immunocompromised patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): Any antibiotic may cause this phenomenon, although the quinolones such as ciprofloxacin seem to be the highest risk, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of inappropriate preoperative skin shaving timing (e.g., the night before)?
back: The Surgical Site Infection (SSI) rate may be doubled compared to shaving immediately before surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): Preoperative skin shaving should be undertaken in the operating theatre immediately before surgery as the SSI rate after clean wound surgery may be doubled if shaving is performed the night before.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is the use of silk sutures inappropriate for skin closure?
back: It leads to suture abscesses because the material logarithmically reduces the number of organisms needed to start an infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): If there is a silk suture in tissue, the critical number of organisms needed to start an infection is reduced logarithmically. Silk should not be used to close skin as it causes suture abscesses for this reason.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why are alcoholic hand gels inappropriate for hygiene during a Clostridium difficile outbreak?
back: Alcoholic hand gels do not destroy the resistant spores of Clostridium difficile.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 72 (Book Page): Alcoholic hand gels can act as a substitute for hand washing, but do not destroy the spores of Clostridium difficile, which may cause pseudomembranous colitis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of continuing prophylactic antibiotics beyond the initial induction dose?
back: It provides no additional infection prevention and encourages the development of bacterial resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What two consequences arise from frequent, illogical changes in empirical antibiotic regimens?
back: 1. Promotion of bacterial resistance. 2. Increased risk of complications like C. difficile enteritis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): change of antibiotics promotes resistance and risks complications, such as C. difficile enteritis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is antibiotic prophylaxis inappropriate if administered after the 4-hour 'decisive period'?
back: The strategy becomes ineffective because bacterial growth has already become established in the tissues.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 67 (Book Page): This interval is called the ‘decisive period’ and strategies aimed at preventing infection from taking a hold become ineffective after this time period.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of inappropriate primary closure in heavily contaminated or 'dirty' wounds?
back: Extremely high infection rates (up to 40%). Delayed primary or secondary closure is indicated.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page)/74: Delayed primary, or secondary, closure remains useful in heavily contaminated wounds. [Table 5.4] Dirty (pus or perforation) Infection rate without prophylaxis 40%.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of using broad-spectrum antibiotics without tight local policies/control?
back: Emergence of multi-drug resistant organisms, specifically MRSA, GRE, and ESBL-producing bacteria.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): often bacteria develop resistance through the acquisition of b-lactamases... the emergence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and glycopeptide-resistant enterococci (GRE).

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary consequence of indiscriminate antibiotic use in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back:
• Encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.
• Provides little to no clinical value as infection rates are already low.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): The use of prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery is of less value as infection rates are low and the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Which biochemical mechanism is most commonly responsible for bacterial resistance to penicillin?
back:
• Acquisition of ̢̢β-lactamases.
• These enzymes break the β-lactam ring in the antibiotic's molecular structure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): Often bacteria develop resistance through the acquisition of β-lactamases, which break up the β-lactam ring present in the molecular structure of many antibiotics.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is the emergence of Extended Spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) in Gram-negative organisms a major concern?
back:
• Confers resistance to many antibiotics (especially cephalosporins).
• Makes finding an effective treatment for urinary tract infections extremely difficult.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): The acquisition of extended spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) is an increasing concern in some gram-negative organisms that cause urinary tract infections because it is difficult to find an antibiotic effective against them.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Pathophysiologically, how does inappropriate antibiotic use trigger Pseudomembranous colitis?
back:
• Destruction of normal colonic bacterial flora.
• Allows overgrowth of commensal Clostridium difficile to pathological, toxin-producing levels.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page)-66: Clostridium difficile is the cause of pseudomembranous colitis, where destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora by antibiotic therapy allows an overgrowth of the normal gut commensal C. diff to pathological levels.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Which antibiotic class carries the highest risk for inducing C. difficile colitis in elderly patients?
back: • Quinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): Any antibiotic may cause this phenomenon, although the quinolones such as ciprofloxacin seem to be the highest risk, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: List three systemic toxicities associated with novel antibiotics like linezolid or teicoplanin.
back:
1. Marrow toxicity.
2. Hepatic toxicity.
3. Renal toxicity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): ...all are relatively expensive, and some have side effects involving marrow, hepatic and renal toxicity. Their use is justified but needs to be controlled by tight local policies...

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is a specific risk of using prolonged and frequently changing antibiotic regimens in surgical patients?
back: • Opportunistic infections, particularly with fungi.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): Opportunistic infection with fungi is an example, particularly when prolonged and changing antibiotic regimes have been used.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: How do biofilms produced by S. epidermidis affect the treatment of prosthetic infections?
back:
• Biofilms adhere to prosthetic surfaces.
• They limit the effectiveness and penetration of antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): The bacteria form biofilms which adhere to prosthetic surfaces and limit the effectiveness of antibiotics.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the clinical consequence of frequently changing antibiotics when a patient shows poor initial response?
back:
• Promotes antibiotic resistance.
• Increases the risk of complications like C. difficile enteritis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): It is illogical to withhold antibiotics until results are available but, if clinical response is poor by the time sensitivities are known, then antibiotics can be changed. Such changes are unusual if the empirical choice of antibiotics is sensible; change of antibiotics promotes resistance and risks complications, such as C. difficile enteritis.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Aside from MRSA, which specific resistant organism is a major concern in general surgical practice?
back: • Glycopeptide-resistant enterococci (GRE).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): ...there is increasing concern about the rising resistance of many other bacteria to antibiotics, in particular the emergence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and glycopeptide-resistant enterococci (GRE).

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the primary consequence of indiscriminate antibiotic use in clean, non-prosthetic surgery?
back: The emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): The use of prophylactic antibiotics in clean, non-prosthetic surgery is of less value as infection rates are low and the indiscriminate use of antibiotics simply encourages the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: How do Staphylococci biochemically resist penicillin therapy?
back: Through the acquisition of ̢-lactamases, which break up the antibiotic’s ̢-lactam ring.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 64 (Book Page): Often bacteria develop resistance through the acquisition of ̢-lactamases, which break up the ̢-lactam ring present in the molecular structure of many antibiotics.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What severe colonic condition is caused by antibiotic-induced destruction of normal flora?
back: Pseudomembranous colitis (caused by overgrowth of Clostridium difficile).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 65 (Book Page): Clostridium difficile is the cause of pseudomembranous colitis, where destruction of the normal colonic bacterial flora by antibiotic therapy allows an overgrowth of the normal gut commensal C. diff to pathological levels.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Which antibiotic class carries the highest risk for inducing C. difficile colitis?
back: Quinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin), especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 66 (Book Page): Any antibiotic may cause this phenomenon, although the quinolones such as ciprofloxacin seem to be the highest risk, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the consequence of frequent/prolonged changes in antibiotic regimes in immunocompromised patients?
back: Opportunistic infections, specifically with fungi.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 68 (Book Page): Opportunistic infection with fungi is an example, particularly when prolonged and changing antibiotic regimes have been used.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: Why is continuing prophylactic antibiotics after surgery considered inappropriate?
back: It provides no value and strictly encourages the development of antibiotic resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 74 (Book Page): There is no evidence that further doses of antibiotics after surgery are of any value in prophylaxis against infection and the practice can only encourage the development of antibiotic resistance.

category: Recognize the consequences of inappropriate use
front: Q: What is the clinical implication of Extended Spectrum ̢-lactamases (ESBLs) in Gram-negative bacilli?
back: They confer resistance to many antibiotics, particularly cephalosporins, making treatment difficult.
